title: Robert Hooke and the Discovery of Cells
subject: Biology
objective: The man who named the cell left no surviving portrait. Meet Robert Hooke, his book Micrographia, his lamp-lit microscope and his count of cork cells.

fill.q: Hooke described cells in his book ____ (1665).
He lit specimens with an oil lamp and a water-filled glass ____.
Hooke saw only the cell ____ in cork.
He estimated about 1.26 ____ cells in one cubic inch of cork.

tf.q: Hooke used a compound microscope he designed.
tf.explain: He built and improved it himself.

tf.q: Hooke saw nuclei in cork cells.
tf.explain: Cork cells are dead; only walls remain.

tf.q: Micrographia was a book of drawings of tiny things seen through a microscope.
tf.explain: It was a bestseller of its time.

tf.q: Hooke studied living pond-water organisms first.

ar.a: Hooke could count cells in cork.
ar.r: Cork cells looked like separate boxes in rows.
ar.explain: The box-like pattern made estimating possible.

ar.a: Hooke saw the nucleus in cork cells.
ar.explain: A is false; R is true.

mcq.q: Why did Hooke need a water-filled globe?
options: to focus light on the specimen

short.q: Why is Hooke's work a turning point in biology?
short.solution: For the first time living material was seen to be built of small units. He named them cells, starting the study that led to cell theory.

short.q: Why could Hooke see walls but not cell contents?
short.solution: Cork is dead tissue; the living contents had disappeared, and his microscope could not show fine detail anyway.

match.explain: Hooke's tools and careful counting made the discovery.
